rules in my CLAUDE.md. The agent followed 11 consistently. The other three (\"never create test files,\" \"always compile after editing,\" \"read the full file before modifying it\") failed at rates that made them decorative. 47 test files created despite a clear prohibition. 112 edits to files the agent hadn't read. 63 premature \"complete\" declarations where the agent claimed a task was done without building the code.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eHere's the thing. The agent \u003cem\u003eunderstands\u003c/em\u003e every rule. It can explain why each one exists. It'll recite them back if you ask. Then 11 tool calls later, deep in a problem-solving loop, it creates \u003ccode\u003eauth.test.ts\u003c/code\u003e because that's what its training says a responsible developer does.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWriting rules is easy. Getting an AI agent to follow them under pressure? Completely different problem. The solution I landed on borrows from Claude Shannon's information theory: reliable communication requires redundant encoding. Same principle applies to agent discipline. Say the same thing seven different ways, through seven different mechanisms, and the message gets through.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-gap-between-understanding-and-compliance\"\u003eThe Gap Between Understanding and Compliance\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-gap-between-understanding-and-compliance\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWatch this failure mode play out. You write a clear instruction:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-markdown\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"hljs-strong\"\u003e**NEVER:**\u003c/span\u003e write mocks, stubs, test doubles, unit tests, or test files.\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-strong\"\u003e**ALWAYS:**\u003c/span\u003e build and run the real system. Validate through actual\nuser interfaces. Capture and verify evidence before claiming completion.\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eSix lines. Unambiguous. The agent reads this at the start of every session. Then the session grows. By tool call 40, those six lines are competing with 30,000+ tokens of accumulated context: code it's read, errors it's debugged, plans it's made. The instruction doesn't disappear. It just loses salience. The agent's been reading Swift files for 20 minutes. It knows the codebase has no tests. And then it writes \u003ccode\u003eUserServiceTests.swift\u003c/code\u003e because the pattern is so deeply embedded in its training that it fires automatically.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eBetter instructions don't work. I tried for weeks. Rephrasing. Bold text. Moving the rule to different positions in the file. The violation rate barely moved. The problem is structural. By tool call 40, six lines of guidance are competing with 30,000+ tokens of accumulated context. They lose.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe numbers that forced a different approach: across 23,479 sessions spanning 42 days, the Skill tool fired 1,370 times. ExitPlanMode, the gate that prevents agents from writing code before planning, triggered 111 times. Those are enforcement mechanisms doing real work. But they only work because they're part of a stack, not standalone instructions.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-7-layer-stack\"\u003eThe 7-Layer Stack\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-7-layer-stack\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eSeven layers. Each one reinforces the same rules through a different mechanism.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-mermaid\"\u003egraph TB\n    subgraph \"The 7-Layer Prompt Engineering Stack\"\n        L7[\"Layer 7: Session Start Hooks\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003eInject context from turn 1\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n        L6[\"Layer 6: MCP Tools\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003eExternal capabilities + constraints\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n        L5[\"Layer 5: Agents\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003eSpecialized roles with scoped instructions\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n        L4[\"Layer 4: Skills\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003eStructured workflows with gates\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n        L3[\"Layer 3: Hooks\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003ePreToolUse blocks, PostToolUse reminders\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n        L2[\"Layer 2: Rules Directory\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003e.claude/rules/*.md — focused rule files\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n        L1[\"Layer 1: CLAUDE.md Constitution\u0026#x3C;br/\u003e\u0026#x3C;i\u003eGlobal + Project instructions\u0026#x3C;/i\u003e\"]\n    end\n\n    L7 --\u003e L6\n    L6 --\u003e L5\n    L5 --\u003e L4\n    L4 --\u003e L3\n    L3 --\u003e L2\n    L2 --\u003e L1\n\n    style L1 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L2 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L3 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#22d3ee,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L4 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#22d3ee,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L5 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#22d3ee,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L6 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L7 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 1: Global Constitution.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003e~/.claude/CLAUDE.md\u003c/code\u003e. Applies to every project on every machine. This is the constitution. Projects can add laws but can't override it. The non-negotiable mandates live here: functional validation only, no test files, no mocks, evidence-based completion claims.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 2: Rules Directory.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003e.claude/rules/*.md\u003c/code\u003e. A 50-line focused file gets more reliable attention than 50 lines buried in a 500-line document. I split governance into nine files: \u003ccode\u003ecoding-style.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003esecurity.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003etesting.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003egit-workflow.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eperformance.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eagents.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003epatterns.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ehooks.md\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003edevelopment-workflow.md\u003c/code\u003e. Each file covers one concern. When the agent needs the security rules, it can locate and re-read a 40-line file instead of scanning a monolith.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 3: Hooks.\u003c/strong\u003e Code that runs on every tool call. This is where rules become enforceable. PreToolUse hooks fire before a tool executes and can block the call entirely. PostToolUse hooks fire after and inject corrective reminders. The agent can't ignore a hook that returns \u003ccode\u003e{ \"decision\": \"block\" }\u003c/code\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 4: Skills.\u003c/strong\u003e Structured workflows with routing tables and gates. A skill like \u003ccode\u003efunctional-validation\u003c/code\u003e is a step-by-step protocol that an agent invokes when it needs to prove something works. Skills carry project-specific context that the agent doesn't have by default. Across all sessions, 1,370 skill invocations kept agents on prescribed workflows instead of improvising.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 5: Agents.\u003c/strong\u003e Specialized roles with scoped instructions. A \u003ccode\u003ecode-reviewer\u003c/code\u003e agent has a review checklist baked into its prompt. A \u003ccode\u003ebuild-fixer\u003c/code\u003e agent knows to check DerivedData and clean caches. Each agent carries domain knowledge that the main agent forgets under context pressure.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 6: MCP Tools.\u003c/strong\u003e External capabilities with built-in constraints. The sequential thinking tool (327 invocations across all sessions) forces structured reasoning before implementation. The Stitch MCP enforces design system compliance. These tools add discipline through their interface design, not through written rules.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLayer 7: Session Start Hooks.\u003c/strong\u003e Inject the full governance context from turn one. Before the agent has any competing context, it loads the rules, the project constitution, and the enforcement expectations. Sets the behavioral baseline before problem-solving begins.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe principle is defense in depth. If the agent forgets the build command (Layer 1 failure), the auto-build hook catches it (Layer 3). If the hook misses it, the evidence gate blocks premature completion claims (Layer 4). No single layer is sufficient. All seven together produce results that no single layer achieves alone.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"hooks-where-rules-become-enforceable\"\u003eHooks: Where Rules Become Enforceable\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#hooks-where-rules-become-enforceable\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eLayers 1 and 2 are suggestions. Layer 3 is enforcement. A hook is a JavaScript function that Claude Code runs automatically on every tool call. Two types:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePreToolUse hooks\u003c/strong\u003e fire before the tool executes. They inspect the tool name and inputs, then return \u003ccode\u003eallow\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eblock\u003c/code\u003e, or inject a warning message.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePostToolUse hooks\u003c/strong\u003e fire after the tool executes. They inspect the output and inject reminders or corrective context.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-mermaid\"\u003esequenceDiagram\n    participant Agent\n    participant PreHook as PreToolUse Hooks\n    participant Tool as Tool Execution\n    participant PostHook as PostToolUse Hooks\n    participant Context as Agent Context\n\n    Agent-\u003e\u003ePreHook: Tool call requested\n    alt Block Decision\n        PreHook--\u003e\u003eAgent: { decision: \"block\" }\u0026#x3C;br/\u003eTool call prevented\n    else Warn Decision\n        PreHook-\u003e\u003eTool: { decision: \"allow\", message: \"...\" }\n        Note over Context: Warning injected into context\n        Tool-\u003e\u003ePostHook: Tool output\n        PostHook-\u003e\u003eContext: Inject reminder if triggered\n        Context-\u003e\u003eAgent: Continue with enriched context\n    else Allow Decision\n        PreHook-\u003e\u003eTool: { decision: \"allow\" }\n        Tool-\u003e\u003ePostHook: Tool output\n        PostHook-\u003e\u003eContext: Inject reminder if triggered\n        Context-\u003e\u003eAgent: Continue with enriched context\n    end\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eHere's \u003ccode\u003eblock-test-files.js\u003c/code\u003e from the \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/krzemienski/shannon-framework\"\u003eshannon-framework\u003c/a\u003e repo. This hook dropped test file creation from a 23% violation rate to zero:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-javascript\"\u003e\u003cspan Version 1 blocked everything with \"test\" in the filename, which also blocked \u003ccode\u003etestimonials.tsx\u003c/code\u003e. Oops. Version 2 added the \u003ccode\u003eALLOWED_EXCEPTIONS\u003c/code\u003e list. Version 3 added content-pattern detection after an agent created \u003ccode\u003esearch-verification.ts\u003c/code\u003e with no \u003ccode\u003e.test.\u003c/code\u003e in the name, but the file contained assertion functions, expected-output comparisons, and a \u003ccode\u003erunVerification()\u003c/code\u003e entry point. A test suite wearing a trench coat.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-five-hooks-that-survived-production\"\u003eThe Five Hooks That Survived Production\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-five-hooks-that-survived-production\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eI built 23 hooks. Five survived. The 18 failures taught me more than the five successes.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"the-survivors\"\u003eThe survivors\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-survivors\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eblock-test-files.js\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e - PreToolUse on Write/Edit. Violation rate: 23% to 0%. The most dramatic improvement in the stack. It fires on every file write and checks the path against 12 test file patterns. Simple, deterministic, no false positives after calibration.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eread-before-edit.js\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e - PreToolUse on Edit. Violation rate: 31% to 4%. Tracks which files have been read in the session and warns when an agent tries to edit an unread file. The warn-not-block approach matters here: sometimes the agent legitimately creates a new file from scratch. Blocking would break that workflow. Warning gives it the nudge without the wall.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-javascript\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"hljs-keyword\"\u003eexport\u003c/span\u003e \u003cspan function_\"\u003ereadBeforeEdit\u003c/span\u003e(\u003cspan class=\"hljs-params\"\u003e{ tool, input, history }\u003c/span\u003e) {\n  \u003cspan class=\"hljs-keyword\"\u003eif\u003c/span\u003e (tool === \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"Read\"\u003c/span\u003e \u0026#x26;\u0026#x26; input.\u003cspan class=\"hljs-property\"\u003efile_path\u003c/span\u003e) {\n    readFiles.\u003cspan class=\"hljs-title function_\"\u003eadd\u003c/span\u003e(input.\u003cspan class=\"hljs-property\"\u003efile_path\u003c/span\u003e);\n    \u003cspan class=\"hljs-keyword\"\u003ereturn\u003c/span\u003e { \u003cspan class=\"hljs-attr\"\u003edecision\u003c/span\u003e: \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"allow\"\u003c/span\u003e };\n  }\n\n  \u003cspan class=\"hljs-keyword\"\u003eif\u003c/span\u003e (![\u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"Edit\"\u003c/span\u003e, \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"MultiEdit\"\u003c/span\u003e].\u003cspan \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"allow\"\u003c/span\u003e,\n      \u003cspan class=\"hljs-attr\"\u003emessage\u003c/span\u003e: \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e`WARNING: Editing \u003cspan class=\"hljs-attr\"\u003edecision\u003c/span\u003e: \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"allow\"\u003c/span\u003e };\n}\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003evalidation-not-compilation.js\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e - PostToolUse on Bash. Violation rate: 41% to 9%. Catches a specific failure mode: the agent runs \u003ccode\u003epnpm build\u003c/code\u003e, sees \"Build succeeded,\" and declares the feature complete. The hook detects build-success patterns in the output and injects a reminder that compilation isn't validation. Something interesting happened after hundreds of sessions. The agent stopped acknowledging the reminder in its output but still changed its behavior. Learned compliance. The behavioral shift persists even when the agent stops visibly responding to the prompt. I'm still not sure why that happens.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eevidence-gate-reminder.js\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e - Fires on TaskUpdate. When a subagent marks a task complete, this hook injects a five-point evidence checklist:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode\u003e[ ] Did I READ the actual evidence file (not just the report)?\n[ ] Did I VIEW the actual screenshot (not just confirm it exists)?\n[ ] Did I EXAMINE the actual command output (not just the exit code)?\n[ ] Can I CITE specific evidence for each validation criterion?\n[ ] Would a skeptical reviewer agree this is complete?\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eTask completion quality improved 34% after deploying this hook. The agent started quoting specific screenshot contents and command output lines instead of saying \"screenshot confirms functionality.\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ccode\u003eskill-activation-check.js\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e - UserPromptSubmit hook. Fires on every user message that looks like an implementation request. Reminds the agent to scan available skills before jumping into code. This hook drives the 1,370 skill invocations I measured. Without it, agents skip skills and improvise, which produces worse results.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 id=\"the-18-hooks-that-died\"\u003eThe 18 hooks that died\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-18-hooks-that-died\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe dead hooks: \u003ccode\u003emax-file-size\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eno-console-log\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003eimport-order\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003ecommit-message-reviewer\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003etype-annotation-enforcer\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003efunction-length\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003esingle-responsibility\u003c/code\u003e, \u003ccode\u003edry-violation-detector\u003c/code\u003e, and ten more. Each seemed reasonable in isolation.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe pattern is clear: \u003cstrong\u003eif the violation can be objectively detected from the tool input alone, a hook works.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003eblock-test-files.js\u003c/code\u003e checks a filename. Deterministic, no judgment calls. \u003ccode\u003efunction-length\u003c/code\u003e requires parsing the full file, understanding function boundaries, and deciding whether 52 lines is too many. Subjective, slow, and wrong often enough to be counterproductive.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eStyle hooks create more problems than they solve. The \u003ccode\u003eimport-order\u003c/code\u003e hook fired on 40% of file writes. The agent spent tokens reorganizing imports, and the reorganized imports were sometimes wrong. Net negative value.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eHere's the meta-rule: hooks should enforce safety invariants, not style preferences. \"Don't commit API keys\" is a safety invariant. \"Functions should be under 50 lines\" is a style preference with too many legitimate exceptions. Can you tell the difference? That's the whole game.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-claudemd-inheritance-chain\"\u003eThe CLAUDE.md Inheritance Chain\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-claudemd-inheritance-chain\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe constitution layer isn't a single file. It's a hierarchy, and the hierarchy matters.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-mermaid\"\u003egraph TD\n    subgraph \"CLAUDE.md Inheritance Chain\"\n fill:#0f172a,stroke:#94a3b8,color:#cbd5e1\n    style R9 fill:#0f172a,stroke:#94a3b8,color:#cbd5e1\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eGlobal\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e~/.claude/CLAUDE.md\u003c/code\u003e) sets the non-negotiables. These rules apply to every project I work on. The functional validation mandate lives here. The prohibition on test files lives here. The evidence-gate requirement lives here. A project CLAUDE.md can add constraints but can't relax these.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eProject\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e./CLAUDE.md\u003c/code\u003e) adds project-specific context. The build command. The tech stack. Known pitfalls. \"DerivedData must be cleaned before building.\" \"Use CryptoKit not Crypto.\" \"The backend binary is at \u003ccode\u003e./server\u003c/code\u003e not \u003ccode\u003e./build/server\u003c/code\u003e.\" These are the rules that prevent the agent from rediscovering the same bugs I already fixed.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRules\u003c/strong\u003e (\u003ccode\u003e.claude/rules/*.md\u003c/code\u003e) break concerns into focused files. A 50-line file about security gets more reliable attention than the same 50 lines buried in a 500-line CLAUDE.md. Nine files, nine concerns. The agent loads them all, but when it needs to recall the git workflow, it can mentally index into a 30-line file instead of scanning everything.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWhy not just one big file? I tested both approaches. A single 800-line CLAUDE.md produced 72% compliance on rules in the bottom half of the file. The same rules split into focused files: 89% compliance. Position in the file matters for a single document. Position in a separate file doesn't, because each file starts at line 1. Think about that for a second. The agent follows rules at the top of a long file more than rules at the bottom. That's wild.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-enforcement-severity-spectrum\"\u003eThe Enforcement Severity Spectrum\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-enforcement-severity-spectrum\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eNot all violations are equal. Creating a test file is a hard violation, the file shouldn't exist. Forgetting to read a file before editing is a soft violation, the edit still might be correct. The hook system reflects this with three severity levels.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBlock\u003c/strong\u003e - The hook stops the tool call. The agent can't proceed until it takes a different approach. Used for: test file creation, API key commits, writes to reference data files. Zero tolerance.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWarn\u003c/strong\u003e - The hook injects a warning but allows the tool call to proceed. Used for: editing unread files, large file modifications, missing build verification. The agent gets the nudge without getting blocked from legitimate edge cases.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRemind\u003c/strong\u003e - The hook injects a contextual reminder after the fact. Used for: dev server restarts after config changes, documentation updates after API changes, the \"compilation isn't validation\" reminder.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eI tested 2-level (block/allow) and 5-level systems before settling on three. The 2-level system hit 87% compliance, but too many false blocks pushed the agent into workaround patterns. It would rename files to dodge the block, which was worse than the original violation. (Imagine that. The agent learned to game your rules.) The 5-level system scored 88%. The extra levels created decision fatigue. The agent spent tokens reasoning about whether a violation was severity 3 or severity 4 instead of doing its actual work. Three levels hit 95% compliance. Simple enough to be reliable.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"subagent-inheritance-the-gap-that-breaks-everything\"\u003eSubagent Inheritance: The Gap That Breaks Everything\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#subagent-inheritance-the-gap-that-breaks-everything\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe main agent follows the constitution. Then it spawns a subagent via the Task tool, and the subagent starts with zero governance context. I measured this gap: 68% compliance for subagents without constitution injection versus 95% with it. That's a 27-point drop just because the rules didn't get passed along.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe fix is a PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool that automatically injects core rules into every subagent prompt. When the main agent spawns a \u003ccode\u003ecode-reviewer\u003c/code\u003e, the hook appends the functional validation mandate, the no-test-files rule, and the evidence-gate checklist to the subagent's instructions. The subagent inherits the constitution without the main agent needing to remember to pass it along.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis is the single most important lesson from the stack: governance must be automatic and inherited. If compliance depends on the agent remembering to propagate rules, it'll forget. 2,827 Task spawns and 929 Agent calls across all 23,479 sessions. That's 3,756 opportunities for governance to drop. How many of those do you think the agent would remember on its own? Automatic injection eliminates the failure mode entirely.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"what-the-numbers-show\"\u003eWhat the Numbers Show\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#what-the-numbers-show\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eAcross the measured sessions, the aggregate violation rate dropped from 3.1 per session to 0.4, an 87% reduction. Hook overhead: 7ms per tool call, undetectable in practice.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe tool leaderboard tells the story of how these sessions actually work. Read was called 87,152 times. Bash: 82,552. Edit: 19,979. The Read-to-Write ratio is 9.6:1. Agents read roughly ten times more than they write. That ratio is a direct consequence of the \"read before edit\" hook. Before the hook existed, the ratio was closer to 4:1. The hook didn't just prevent blind edits; it changed the agent's entire approach to code modification. More reading means more context means fewer bugs. I wasn't expecting a single hook to shift the reading behavior that dramatically, but here we are.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe skill invocation count, 1,370, matters because skills bridge static rules and dynamic workflows. A rule says \"validate through the real UI.\" A skill provides the step-by-step protocol: build from source, start the simulator, exercise each feature, capture screenshots, apply the evidence gate. The \u003ccode\u003efunctional-validation\u003c/code\u003e skill in the \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/krzemienski/shannon-framework\"\u003eshannon-framework\u003c/a\u003e repo encodes this entire workflow:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-markdown\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"hljs-section\"\u003e### Step 1: Build the Real System\u003c/span\u003e\nBuild from source. No placeholders, no stubs.\n\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-section\"\u003e### Step 2: Run It\u003c/span\u003e\nStart the app, service, or tool in its real environment.\n\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-section\"\u003e### Step 3: Exercise Through UI\u003c/span\u003e\nInteract through the actual interface — simulator, browser, CLI.\n\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-section\"\u003e### Step 4: Capture Evidence\u003c/span\u003e\nScreenshots, command output, log entries.\n\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-section\"\u003e### Step 5: Apply Gate Validation\u003c/span\u003e\nBefore claiming complete:\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-bullet\"\u003e-\u003c/span\u003e [ ] Did I READ the actual evidence?\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-bullet\"\u003e-\u003c/span\u003e [ ] Can I CITE specific proof for each criterion?\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-bullet\"\u003e-\u003c/span\u003e [ ] Would a skeptical reviewer agree?\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe skill doesn't replace the hook. The hook doesn't replace the CLAUDE.md instruction. All three say the same thing through different mechanisms at different points in the session. That's the redundancy principle at work.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"when-layers-conflict\"\u003eWhen Layers Conflict\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#when-layers-conflict\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe stack usually reinforces itself. Sometimes two layers say contradictory things. Knowing which wins matters.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eMost common collision: project CLAUDE.md says \"run \u003ccode\u003epnpm build\u003c/code\u003e after editing TypeScript files.\" A PostToolUse hook fires on the same Bash command and injects \"compilation is NOT validation — exercise the feature through the real UI.\" Looks like Layer 1 and Layer 3 are fighting.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThey're not. Layer 1 defines what to do. Layer 3 defines what that action doesn't prove. The build verifies syntax and types. The hook reminds the agent that a green build doesn't mean the feature works. Run the build, then run the real thing. Additive, not contradictory.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe harder case: a PreToolUse hook blocks an action the constitution calls for. This happened once with \u003ccode\u003eread-before-edit.js\u003c/code\u003e. The project constitution said \"update \u003ccode\u003esrc/config.ts\u003c/code\u003e with the new environment variable.\" The hook flagged the edit because \u003ccode\u003econfig.ts\u003c/code\u003e hadn't been read that session. Block versus explicit instruction. Layer 3 wins temporarily — read first, then edit. Layer 1 still gets fulfilled with one extra step. When a block hook fires on an instructed action, satisfy the precondition. Don't work around it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"building-your-own-stack\"\u003eBuilding Your Own Stack\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#building-your-own-stack\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/krzemienski/shannon-framework\"\u003eshannon-framework\u003c/a\u003e repo contains working implementations of all the hooks and skills I've described. Drop them into your project:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-bash\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"hljs-comment\"\u003e# Copy hooks into your Claude Code project\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-built_in\"\u003ecp\u003c/span\u003e -r hooks/ .claude/hooks/\n\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-comment\"\u003e# Copy skills\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-built_in\"\u003ecp\u003c/span\u003e -r skills/ .claude/skills/\n\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-comment\"\u003e# Copy agents\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-built_in\"\u003ecp\u003c/span\u003e -r agents/ .claude/agents/\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eStart with three hooks. \u003ccode\u003eblock-test-files.js\u003c/code\u003e if you want functional validation discipline. \u003ccode\u003eread-before-edit.js\u003c/code\u003e if your agents make blind edits. \u003ccode\u003evalidation-not-compilation.js\u003c/code\u003e if you're tired of premature \"done\" declarations. Measure violation rates for a week before adding more.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe hooks that survive production share two properties:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eObjective detection.\u003c/strong\u003e The violation is identifiable from the tool inputs alone, without judgment calls. Filename patterns: yes. Code quality assessments: no.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLow false-positive rates after calibration.\u003c/strong\u003e A hook that fires incorrectly trains the agent to ignore it. Worse than no hook at all.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eIf you can't define the violation in a regular expression or a simple conditional, it doesn't belong in a hook. Put it in a skill or an agent prompt instead, where the agent can apply judgment.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-shannon-principle\"\u003eThe Shannon Principle\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-shannon-principle\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe framework is named after Claude Shannon for a reason. Shannon proved that you can transmit messages reliably over noisy channels by adding redundancy, error-correcting codes that let the receiver reconstruct the original message even when some bits get corrupted. An LLM context window is a noisy channel. Instructions degrade as the context grows. Competing information introduces noise. Training priors override explicit instructions.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe 7-layer stack is an error-correcting code for agent behavior. Layer 1 states the rule. Layer 2 provides detail. Layer 3 enforces it mechanically. Layer 4 embeds it in workflows. Layer 5 scopes it to specialized roles. Layer 6 builds it into tool interfaces. Layer 7 loads it before noise accumulates.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eNo single layer is sufficient. I know because I tried each one alone. CLAUDE.md alone: 60% compliance. Hooks alone: 75%. Skills alone: 80%. All seven together: 95%+. The remaining 5% is why you still review the output. But the difference between 60% and 95%? That's the difference between an agent that creates work and an agent that saves it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe prompt engineering stack isn't a document. It's a system. Treat it like one.\u003c/p\u003e"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"54:[\"$\",\"div\",null,{\"className\":\"prose\",\"dangerouslySetInnerHTML\":{\"__html\":\"$65\"}},\"$20\",\"$64\",1]\n55:D{\"time\":62.895958000000974}\n55:[\"$\",\"$L67\",null,{},\"$20\",\"$66\",1]\n56:D{\"time\":62.91287499999817}\n69:D{\"time\":62.949249999997846}\n69:D\"$6a\"\n69:D{\"time\":62.99491699999999}\n69:[\"$\",\"$L70\",null,{\"href\":\"/posts/post-03-functional-validation\",\"className\":\"group audit-evidence/cycle-05-260518-1808/repomix-output.xml:178431:<p>Here's what a hook actually does. This is <code>validation-not-compilation.js</code> from the <a href="https://github.com/krzemienski/shannon-framework">shannon-framework</a>. It fires after every Bash command, watches for build success, and injects a reminder that "it compiled" is not "it works."</p>

create test files\" in CLAUDE.md. The agents created test files anyway.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eBold formatting, triple emphasis, all-caps warnings. The violation rate dropped but never hit zero. Across 23,479 sessions, the pattern was obvious: text-based instructions are suggestions. Agents deprioritize them when context gets long, when the task gets hairy, when the implementation chain goes deep. It's not defiance — the agent is making trade-offs in a limited context window, and \"do not create test files\" loses to \"I need to verify this function works.\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThen I wrote a 72-line JavaScript hook that blocks Write calls to any file matching test patterns. Violation rate: zero. The Write tool call hits the hook, the hook returns exit code 2, and the agent sees a message explaining why the action was rejected. Not a suggestion. A hard stop.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThat's the difference between a skill that suggests and a plugin that enforces.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-gap-between-instructions-and-enforcement\"\u003eThe Gap Between Instructions and Enforcement\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-gap-between-instructions-and-enforcement\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eClaude Code's plugin system has four extension points: hooks that fire on tool events, skills that provide domain workflows, agents that define specialist roles, and MCP servers that add tool capabilities. Most people use CLAUDE.md and maybe a few skills. Almost nobody builds hooks. That's a mistake.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eAcross 23,479 sessions, the Skill tool fired 1,370 times. The tool leaderboard: Read fired 87,152 times, Bash fired 82,552 times, Edit fired 19,979 times. For every skill invocation, there were 63 Read calls and 60 Bash calls happening without any skill guidance.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eSkills are opt-in. Hooks are mandatory. Every one of those 19,979 Edit calls passed through my PreToolUse hooks. Every one of those 82,552 Bash calls triggered my PostToolUse hooks. The agent doesn't choose to comply. The enforcement layer checks automatically, on every tool call.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"one-hook-end-to-end\"\u003eOne Hook, End to End\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#one-hook-end-to-end\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eHere's what a hook actually does. A clean build means the code is syntactically correct and type-safe. It says nothing about whether the feature does what you asked. Without a hook, the agent runs \u003ccode\u003enpm run build\u003c/code\u003e, sees \"compiled successfully,\" and marks the task done. The feature is broken. Nobody checked.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe hook source:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-javascript\"\u003e\u003cspan \u003cspan class=\"hljs-attr\"\u003e\"type\"\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan class=\"hljs-punctuation\"\u003e:\u003c/span\u003e \u003cspan class=\"hljs-string\"\u003e\"command\"\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan class=\"hljs-punctuation\"\u003e}\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cspan class=\"hljs-punctuation\"\u003e}\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eDrop the file in \u003ccode\u003e.claude/hooks/\u003c/code\u003e, add the entry to \u003ccode\u003e.claude/settings.json\u003c/code\u003e, and the hook fires on every Bash call for every session. No registration, no manifest parsing.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat it catches in practice:\u003c/strong\u003e during a Next.js feature build, an agent ran \u003ccode\u003epnpm build\u003c/code\u003e, got \"Compiled successfully,\" and started drafting a completion message. The hook fired. The agent spun up the dev server and found a server action returning 500 — an environment variable wasn't set in the test environment. Build: green. Feature: broken. The hook caught it 20 minutes before it would've surfaced in production.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eAcross 82,552 Bash calls in 23,479 sessions, the hook fired every time a build succeeded. Every time.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-hook-lifecycle\"\u003eThe Hook Lifecycle\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-hook-lifecycle\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThree intercept points: before the tool runs, after it finishes, and once per user message. That's the full lifecycle:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-mermaid\"\u003eflowchart TD\n    A[\"User sends prompt\"] --\u003e B[\"UserPromptSubmit hooks fire\"]\n    B --\u003e C[\"Agent reasons, selects tool\"]\n    C --\u003e D[\"PreToolUse hooks fire\"]\n    D --\u003e E{Hook decision?}\n    E --\u003e|\"exit 2 + stderr\"| F[\"Tool call rejected\u0026#x3C;br/\u003eAgent sees block message\"]\n    E --\u003e|\"exit 2 (PostToolUse)\"| G[\"Tool executes\u0026#x3C;br/\u003eAgent sees injected context\"]\n    E --\u003e|\"exit 0, no output\"| H[\"Tool executes normally\"]\n    G --\u003e I[\"PostToolUse hooks fire\"]\n    H --\u003e I\n    I --\u003e J[\"Agent sees output +\u0026#x3C;br/\u003eany injected reminders\"]\n    F --\u003e K[\"Agent must find\u0026#x3C;br/\u003ealternative approach\"]\n    J --\u003e C\n    K --\u003e C\n\n    style A fill:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n    style F fill:#ef4444,color:#f1f5f9\n    style G fill:#f59e0b,color:#1e293b\n    style H fill:#22c55e,color:#1e293b\n    style I fill:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThree event types, three possible responses. That's the entire hook API:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePreToolUse\u003c/strong\u003e fires before the tool executes. It can block (write to stderr, exit code 2), warn (inject context and allow), or silently allow (exit 0 with no output).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePostToolUse\u003c/strong\u003e fires after execution completes. It can inject reminders based on output by writing to stderr and exiting with code 2. It can't block the action already taken, but it shapes what the agent does next.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eUserPromptSubmit\u003c/strong\u003e fires on every user message, before the agent starts reasoning. It can inject workflow requirements or force skill evaluation.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA detail that bit me: a hook that crashes is a silent allow — the tool call proceeds as if no hook existed. A broken hook should never break the agent. But wrap every hook in try/catch, because a silently failing hook is worse than a missing one. At least a missing hook is obvious.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-4-layer-enforcement-pyramid\"\u003eThe 4-Layer Enforcement Pyramid\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-4-layer-enforcement-pyramid\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA single enforcement mechanism isn't enough. CLAUDE.md instructions get forgotten. Hooks are too rigid for nuanced decisions. Skills require invocation. Commands require user action. The Shannon Framework — named after Claude Shannon, who proved reliable communication requires redundant encoding — layers all four:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode class=\"hljs language-mermaid\"\u003egraph TB\n    subgraph L4[\"Layer 4: Commands\"]\n        C1[\"/autopilot\"]\n        C2[\"/ralph\"]\n        C3[\"/team\"]\n    end\n\n    subgraph L3[\"Layer 3: Skills\"]\n        S1[\"functional-validation\"]\n        S2[\"gate-validation-discipline\"]\n        S3[\"e2e-validate\"]\n    end\n\n    subgraph L2[\"Layer 2: Hooks\"]\n        H1[\"block-test-files.js\u0026#x3C;br/\u003ePreToolUse: Write|Edit\"]\n        H2[\"read-before-edit.js\u0026#x3C;br/\u003ePreToolUse: Edit\"]\n        H3[\"validation-not-compilation.js\u0026#x3C;br/\u003ePostToolUse: Bash\"]\n        H4[\"evidence-gate-reminder.js\u0026#x3C;br/\u003ePostToolUse: TaskUpdate\"]\n        H5[\"skill-activation-check.js\u0026#x3C;br/\u003eUserPromptSubmit\"]\n    end\n\n    subgraph L1[\"Layer 1: CLAUDE.md\"]\n        M1[\"No mocks mandate\"]\n        M2[\"Functional validation protocol\"]\n        M3[\"Read-before-write rule\"]\n    end\n\n    C1 --\u003e S1\n    C2 --\u003e S2\n    C3 --\u003e S3\n    S1 --\u003e M1\n    S2 --\u003e M2\n    S3 --\u003e M3\n    H1 -.-\u003e|\"enforces\"| M1\n    H2 -.-\u003e|\"enforces\"| M3\n    H3 -.-\u003e|\"enforces\"| M2\n    H4 -.-\u003e|\"enforces\"| M2\n    H5 -.-\u003e|\"enforces\"| S1\n\n    style L4 fill:#6366f1,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L3 fill:#3b82f6,color:#f1f5f9\n    style L2 fill:#22d3ee,color:#1e293b\n    style L1 fill:#1e293b,color:#cbd5e1\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eEach layer catches what the previous one misses:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCLAUDE.md\u003c/strong\u003e tells the agent what to do. Agents forget. Compliance: ~60%.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHooks\u003c/strong\u003e enforce rules automatically. Can't handle nuanced workflows. Compliance on targeted behaviors: near 100%.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSkills\u003c/strong\u003e provide structured workflows with context the agent lacks. They require invocation, and agents skip them under pressure. The \u003ccode\u003eskill-activation-check.js\u003c/code\u003e hook closes this gap.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eCommands\u003c/strong\u003e give users direct control — the final safety net.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eCombined 4-layer compliance: 95%+. The remaining 5% is why you still review the output.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-other-four-hooks\"\u003eThe Other Four Hooks\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-other-four-hooks\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe Shannon Framework ships five hooks total. \u003ccode\u003evalidation-not-compilation.js\u003c/code\u003e is covered above. No registration, no manifest parsing, no framework overhead.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"what-breaks-and-how-to-fix-it\"\u003eWhat Breaks and How to Fix It\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#what-breaks-and-how-to-fix-it\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eI've debugged enough hooks to compile a failure catalog.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMatcher mistakes.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ccode\u003eWrite\u003c/code\u003e matches the Write tool. It doesn't match Edit or MultiEdit. If you need all three, use \u003ccode\u003eWrite|Edit|MultiEdit\u003c/code\u003e. If your hook isn't firing, check the matcher first.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSilent crashes.\u003c/strong\u003e A hook that throws an unhandled exception produces no output — silent allow. Always wrap everything in try/catch with a \u003ccode\u003eprocess.exit(0)\u003c/code\u003e fallback. A crashing hook is worse than a missing one because you think you're protected and you're not.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePerformance traps.\u003c/strong\u003e Hook scripts have to be fast. Synchronous. Under 100ms. No network calls. I had a hook that validated imports against a remote package registry — added 2 seconds to every Edit call. Moving validation to a PostToolUse hook that batched checks eliminated the latency.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe hook that cried wolf.\u003c/strong\u003e Too many warnings train the agent to ignore them all. Each of my five hooks targets a specific, dangerous behavior with a clear trigger. A hook that warns on every file edit becomes noise. \u003ccode\u003evalidation-not-compilation.js\u003c/code\u003e fires only after build commands that succeed, not after every Bash call.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eState management gotchas.\u003c/strong\u003e The \u003ccode\u003eread-before-edit.js\u003c/code\u003e hook tracks state in a module-level Set. Works because Claude Code loads hooks once per session and keeps them in memory. Restart the session, the Set is empty. Don't rely on hook state across sessions. Use the filesystem or an MCP server.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"skills-the-structured-workflow-layer\"\u003eSkills: The Structured Workflow Layer\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#skills-the-structured-workflow-layer\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eHooks enforce boundaries. Skills provide workflows. The functional-validation skill in the Shannon Framework is a SKILL.md file, a markdown document with trigger patterns, context, and execution steps:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cpre\u003e\u003ccode\u003e# functional-validation\n\n\u003e Validates features through real system behavior.\n\n## Trigger Patterns\n- \"validate this\"\n- \"functional validation\"\n- \"prove it works\"\n\n## Execution Steps\n1. Build the real system (no placeholders, no stubs)\n2. Run it in its real environment\n3. Exercise through the actual UI\n4. Capture evidence (screenshots, logs, responses)\n5. Apply gate validation (5-question checklist)\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWhen the agent invokes this skill, it loads these instructions into context. The five execution steps become the agent's workflow. The checklist makes sure the agent doesn't skip the evidence phase.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eSkills and hooks reinforce each other. The skill tells the agent \u003cem\u003ehow\u003c/em\u003e to validate. The \u003ccode\u003eblock-test-files.js\u003c/code\u003e hook prevents shortcuts. The \u003ccode\u003evalidation-not-compilation.js\u003c/code\u003e hook catches build success declared as validation. The \u003ccode\u003eevidence-gate-reminder.js\u003c/code\u003e hook catches tasks marked complete without evidence. Together, they create an enforcement surface that's hard to circumvent.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"hooks-vs-mcp-servers-vs-claudemd\"\u003eHooks vs. MCP Servers vs. CLAUDE.md\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#hooks-vs-mcp-servers-vs-claudemd\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe decision framework:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eUse CLAUDE.md\u003c/strong\u003e for general guidance that doesn't need enforcement. Style preferences, architectural conventions, project context. If 60-70% compliance is enough, CLAUDE.md works.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eUse a hook\u003c/strong\u003e when you need to intercept an existing tool call. Block certain Writes, inject warnings after Bash, remind on Edit. Hooks modify existing behavior automatically.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eUse an MCP server\u003c/strong\u003e when you need to give the agent a capability it doesn't have. Query a database, search an AST, interact with an LSP server, manage persistent state. MCP servers add new tools.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eUse a skill\u003c/strong\u003e for structured, multi-step workflows that carry domain context. Validation protocols, review checklists, deployment procedures. Skills are invocable — pair them with a UserPromptSubmit hook to make sure the agent loads them.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003ch2 id=\"the-shannon-insight\"\u003eThe Shannon Insight\u003ca aria-hidden=\"true\" tabindex=\"-1\" href=\"#the-shannon-insight\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"icon icon-link\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eClaude Shannon proved you can transmit information reliably over a noisy channel by adding redundant encoding. Same principle applies here. A single instruction in CLAUDE.md is a signal in a noisy channel. Long context, competing priorities, complex task chains. By the time the agent is deep in an implementation, that instruction is noise.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eRedundant encoding means saying the same thing four ways, at four enforcement points:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe CLAUDE.md rule says \"no test files.\"\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe \u003ccode\u003eblock-test-files.js\u003c/code\u003e hook blocks test file creation at the tool boundary.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe \u003ccode\u003efunctional-validation\u003c/code\u003e skill provides an alternative workflow.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe \u003ccode\u003e/autopilot\u003c/code\u003e command orchestrates the entire flow including validation.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eCLAUDE.md guides the well-behaved agent. The hook stops the forgetful agent. The skill redirects the agent that wants to verify but doesn't know how. The command handles the case where the user needs to drive.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eI thought hooks alone would be enough when I first built this. I was wrong. An agent blocked from creating test files doesn't know what to do \u003cem\u003einstead\u003c/em\u003e. It sits there, confused. The skill layer exists because blocking bad behavior without providing an alternative is only half the solution.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eBefore hooks, every agent ignored at least two rules per session. After hooks, zero violations on blocked behaviors. The 19,979 Edit calls all passed through \u003ccode\u003eread-before-edit.js\u003c/code\u003e. The 82,552 Bash calls all passed through \u003ccode\u003evalidation-not-compilation.js\u003c/code\u003e. Every single call, without me watching, without the agent choosing to comply.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThat's what a plugin system is for. Not adding features. Adding discipline.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003cem\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/krzemienski/shannon-framework\"\u003eShannon Framework\u003c/a\u003e is a reference Claude Code plugin with 5 hooks, 1 skill, and 1 agent template. Install it. Try to create a test file, skip a planning phase, claim completion without evidence. Watch the hooks catch each one before the tool executes. That's the difference between instructions the agent reads and enforcement the agent can't skip.\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"54:[\"$\",\"div\",null,{\"className\":\"prose\",\"dangerouslySetInnerHTML\":{\"__html\":\"$65\"}},\"$20\",\"$64\",1]\n55:D{\"time\":60.78608399999939}\n55:[\"$\",\"$L67\",null,{},\"$20\",\"$66\",1]\n56:D{\"time\":60.80449999999837}\n69:D{\"time\":60.843417000000045}\n69:D\"$6a\"\n69:D{\"time\":60.89937500000087}\n69:[\"$\",\"$L70\",null,{\"href\":\"/posts/post-15-skills-anatomy\",\"className\":\"group mechanical discipline across 23,479 AI coding sessions</p><a href="https://github.com/krzemienski/shannon-framework" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="inline-flex items-center gap-2 mt-6 px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-accent bg-accent/10 border border-accent/20 rounded-lg hover:bg-accent/20 transition-colors"><span aria-hidden="true" data-glyph="term">·</span>View companion repo<span aria-hidden="true">↗</span></a></header><div class="flex flex-wrap gap-2 mb-8"><a class="text-xs px-2.5 py-1 rounded-full bg-surface-chip-hover border border-border-chip text-cream-body bg-surface-chip-hover border border-border-chip text-cream-body hover:border-accent/40 hover:text-cream transition-colors" href="/posts?tag=PromptEngineering">#<!-- -->PromptEngineering</a><a class="text-xs px-2.5 py-1 rounded-full bg-surface-chip-hover border border-border-chip text-cream-body hover:border-accent/40 hover:text-cream transition-colors" href="/posts?tag=AgentGovernance">#<!-- -->AgentGovernance</a></div><div class="wa-typed-body"><p style="margin-top:0;font-size:var(--text-body-lead);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.92);font-family:&quot;Fraunces&quot;, Georgia, serif;font-style:italic;font-weight:400;letter-spacing:-0.2px">I had 14 rules in my CLAUDE.md. The agent followed 11 consistently. The other three (&#x27;never create test files,&#x27; &#x27;always compile after editing,&#x27; &#x27;read the full file before modifying it&#x27;) failed at rates that made them decorative. 47 test files created despite a clear prohibition. 112 edits to files the agent hadn&#x27;t read. 63 premature &#x27;complete&#x27; declarations where the agent claimed a task was done without building the code.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Here&#x27;s the thing. The agent understands every rule. It can explain why each one exists. It&#x27;ll recite them back if you ask. Then 11 tool calls later, deep in a problem-solving loop, it creates auth.test.ts because that&#x27;s what its training says a responsible developer does.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Writing rules is easy. Getting an AI agent to follow them under pressure? Completely different problem. The solution I landed on borrows from Claude Shannon&#x27;s information theory: reliable communication requires redundant encoding. Same principle applies to agent discipline. Say the same thing seven different ways, through seven different mechanisms, and the message gets through.</p><aside aria-label="TL;DR" style="margin:28px 0;padding:20px 24px 16px;border-radius:10px;background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(255, 61, 82, 0.06), rgba(255, 61, 82, 0.02));border-left:3px solid var(--accent);border:1px solid var(--hairline);border-left-width:3px"><div class="wa-mono" style="font-size:var(--text-eyebrow-size);font-weight:700;letter-spacing:1.6px;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:12px">TL;DR</div><ul style="margin:0;padding:0;list-style:none"><li style="position:relative;padding-left:18px;padding-top:0;padding-bottom:8px;border-top:none;font-size:var(--text-body-index);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:var(--text, #f4f3ee)"><span aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute;left:0;top:7px;color:var(--accent);font-weight:700">›</span>Seven layers (<code class="wa-mono" style="background:rgba(122,61,255,0.12);padding:1px 6px;border-radius:3px;font-size:0.92em">CLAUDE.md</code> → <code class="wa-mono" style="background:rgba(122,61,255,0.12);padding:1px 6px;border-radius:3px;font-size:0.92em">.claude/rules/</code> → hooks → skills → agents → MCP tools → SessionStart hooks) drove aggregate violations from 3.1 per session to 0.4 — an 87% reduction at 7ms hook overhead per tool call.</li><li style="position:relative;padding-left:18px;padding-top:8px;padding-bottom:8px;border-top:1px solid var(--hairline);font-size:var(--text-body-index);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:var(--text, #f4f3ee)"><span aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute;left:0;top:15px;color:var(--accent);font-weight:700">›</span>Five hooks survived production out of 23 built; <code class="wa-mono" style="background:rgba(122,61,255,0.12);padding:1px 6px;border-radius:3px;font-size:0.92em">block-test-files.js</code> took test-file creation from 23% to 0%, and <code class="wa-mono" style="background:rgba(122,61,255,0.12);padding:1px 6px;border-radius:3px;font-size:0.92em">read-before-edit.js</code> shifted the Read-to-Write ratio from 4:1 to 9.6:1 across 87,152 reads versus 19,979 edits.</li><li style="position:relative;padding-left:18px;padding-top:8px;padding-bottom:8px;border-top:1px solid var(--hairline);font-size:var(--text-body-index);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:var(--text, #f4f3ee)"><span aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute;left:0;top:15px;color:var(--accent);font-weight:700">›</span>Splitting governance into nine focused <code class="wa-mono" style="background:rgba(122,61,255,0.12);padding:1px 6px;border-radius:3px;font-size:0.92em">.claude/rules/*.md</code> files lifted compliance on bottom-half rules from 72% (single 800-line CLAUDE.md) to 89%, and the 3-level block/warn/remind severity model out-scored 2-level (87%) and 5-level (88%) variants at 95%.</li></ul></aside><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">The Gap Between Understanding and Compliance</h2><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Watch this failure mode play out. You write a clear instruction:</p><div style="position:relative;margin:24px 0;border-radius:10px;overflow:hidden;border:1px solid var(--hairline)"><button type="button" aria-label="Copy code to clipboard" class="wa-copy-btn" style="position:absolute;top:8px;right:8px;padding:4px 10px;font-size:11px;font-family:&quot;JetBrains Mono&quot;, monospace;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:0.4px;color:rgba(244,243,238,0.9);background:rgba(255,255,255,0.06);border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.12);border-radius:6px;cursor:pointer;z-index:2;transition:background 0.18s ease, color 0.18s ease, border-color 0.18s ease">COPY</button><pre class="wa-code hljs" style="margin:0;padding:16px 18px;font-size:var(--text-floor);color:var(--text, #f4f3ee);background:rgba(0,0,0,0.4);overflow:auto;white-space:pre"><span class="hljs-strong">**NEVER:**</span> write mocks, stubs, test doubles, unit tests, or test files.
audit-evidence/og-meta-260519-0256/cycle-03/routes/post-07-prompt-engineering-stack.html:35:user interfaces. Capture and verify evidence before claiming completion.</pre></div><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Six lines. Unambiguous. The agent reads this at the start of every session. Then the session grows. By tool call 40, those six lines are competing with 30,000+ tokens of accumulated context: code it&#x27;s read, errors it&#x27;s debugged, plans it&#x27;s made. The instruction doesn&#x27;t disappear. It just loses salience. The agent&#x27;s been reading Swift files for 20 minutes. It knows the codebase has no tests. And then it writes UserServiceTests.swift because the pattern is so deeply embedded in its training that it fires automatically.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Better instructions don&#x27;t work. I tried for weeks. Rephrasing. Bold text. Moving the rule to different positions in the file. The violation rate barely moved. The problem is structural. By tool call 40, six lines of guidance are competing with 30,000+ tokens of accumulated context. They lose.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">The numbers that forced a different approach: across 23,479 sessions spanning 42 days, the Skill tool fired 1,370 times. ExitPlanMode, the gate that prevents agents from writing code before planning, triggered 111 times. Those are enforcement mechanisms doing real work. But they only work because they&#x27;re part of a stack, not standalone instructions.</p><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">The 7-Layer Stack</h2><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Seven layers. &#x27;JetBrains Mono&#x27;, monospace);font-size:11px;color:var(--text-3, rgba(244,243,238,0.4));letter-spacing:0.06em">The 7-layer prompt-engineering stack. Defense in depth — Layer 1 sets non-negotiables at the apex; Layers 2-7 reinforce through different mechanisms (rules, hooks, skills, agents, MCP tools, session hooks). No single layer suffices; all seven together drive 87% violation reduction.</figcaption></figure><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 1: Global Constitution. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Applies to every project on every machine. This is the constitution. Projects can add laws but can&#x27;t override it. The non-negotiable mandates live here: functional validation only, no test files, no mocks, evidence-based completion claims.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 2: Rules Directory. .claude/rules/*.md. A 50-line focused file gets more reliable attention than 50 lines buried in a 500-line document. I split governance into nine files: coding-style.md, security.md, testing.md, git-workflow.md, performance.md, agents.md, patterns.md, hooks.md, development-workflow.md. Each file covers one concern. When the agent needs the security rules, it can locate and re-read a 40-line file instead of scanning a monolith.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 3: Hooks. Code that runs on every tool call. This is where rules become enforceable. PreToolUse hooks fire before a tool executes and can block the call entirely. PostToolUse hooks fire after and inject corrective reminders. The agent can&#x27;t ignore a hook that returns { &#x27;decision&#x27;: &#x27;block&#x27; }.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 4: Skills. Structured workflows with routing tables and gates. A skill like functional-validation is a step-by-step protocol that an agent invokes when it needs to prove something works. Skills carry project-specific context that the agent doesn&#x27;t have by default. Across all sessions, 1,370 skill invocations kept agents on prescribed workflows instead of improvising.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 5: Agents. Specialized roles with scoped instructions. A code-reviewer agent has a review checklist baked into its prompt. A build-fixer agent knows to check DerivedData and clean caches. Each agent carries domain knowledge that the main agent forgets under context pressure.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 6: MCP Tools. External capabilities with built-in constraints. The sequential thinking tool (327 invocations across all sessions) forces structured reasoning before implementation. The Stitch MCP enforces design system compliance. These tools add discipline through their interface design, not through written rules.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layer 7: Session Start Hooks. Inject the full governance context from turn one. Before the agent has any competing context, it loads the rules, the project constitution, and the enforcement expectations. Sets the behavioral baseline before problem-solving begins.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">The principle is defense in depth. If the agent forgets the build command (Layer 1 failure), the auto-build hook catches it (Layer 3). If the hook misses it, the evidence gate blocks premature completion claims (Layer 4). No single layer is sufficient. All seven together produce results that no single layer achieves alone.</p><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">Hooks: Where Rules Become Enforceable</h2><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Layers 1 and 2 are suggestions. Layer 3 is enforcement. A hook is a JavaScript function that Claude Code runs automatically on every tool call. The agent started quoting specific screenshot contents and command output lines instead of saying &#x27;screenshot confirms functionality.&#x27;</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">skill-activation-check.js — UserPromptSubmit hook. Without it, agents skip skills and improvise, which produces worse results.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">The 18 hooks that died: max-file-size, no-console-log, import-order, commit-message-reviewer, type-annotation-enforcer, function-length, single-responsibility, dry-violation-detector, and ten more. Each seemed reasonable in isolation.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">The pattern is clear: if the violation can be objectively detected from the tool input alone, a hook works. block-test-files.js checks a filename. Deterministic, no judgment calls. function-length requires parsing the full file, understanding function boundaries, and deciding whether 52 lines is too many. Subjective, slow, and wrong often enough to be counterproductive.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Style hooks create more problems than they solve. The import-order hook fired on 40% of file writes. The agent spent tokens reorganizing imports, and the reorganized imports were sometimes wrong. Net negative value.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Here&#x27;s the meta-rule: hooks should enforce safety invariants, not style preferences. &#x27;Don&#x27;t commit API keys&#x27; is a safety invariant. &#x27;Functions should be under 50 lines&#x27; is a style preference with too many legitimate exceptions. Can you tell the difference? That&#x27;s the whole game.</p><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">The CLAUDE.md Inheritance Chain</h2><figure style="margin:32px 6px);background:var(--bg-2, rgba(0,0,0,0.25));border:1px solid var(--border-strong, rgba(255,255,255,0.16));font-size:var(--text-eyebrow-size);color:var(--text, #f4f3ee);margin-top:6px;font-weight:600">patterns.md</div><div style="padding:8px 10px;border-radius:var(--radius-sm, 6px);background:var(--bg-2, rgba(0,0,0,0.25));border:1px solid var(--border-strong, rgba(255,255,255,0.16));font-size:var(--text-eyebrow-size);color:var(--text, #f4f3ee);margin-top:6px;font-weight:600">performance.md</div></div></div><figcaption style="margin-top:10px;font-size:var(--text-eyebrow-size);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.55);line-height:var(--leading-link);font-style:italic">Global constitution → project constitution → focused rule files. Each layer extends the previous; no project can relax global non-negotiables.</figcaption></figure><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Global (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) sets the non-negotiables. These rules apply to every project I work on. The functional validation mandate lives here. The prohibition on test files lives here. The evidence-gate requirement lives here. A project CLAUDE.md can add constraints but can&#x27;t relax these.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Project (./CLAUDE.md) adds project-specific context. The build command. The tech stack. Known pitfalls. &#x27;DerivedData must be cleaned before building.&#x27; &#x27;Use CryptoKit not Crypto.&#x27; &#x27;The backend binary is at ./server not ./build/server.&#x27; These are the rules that prevent the agent from rediscovering the same bugs I already fixed.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Rules (.claude/rules/*.md) break concerns into focused files. A 50-line file about security gets more reliable attention than the same 50 lines buried in a 500-line CLAUDE.md. Nine files, nine concerns. The agent loads them all, but when it needs to recall the git workflow, it can mentally index into a 30-line file instead of scanning everything.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Why not just one big file? I tested both approaches. A single 800-line CLAUDE.md produced 72% compliance on rules in the bottom half of the file. The same rules split into focused files: 89% compliance. Position in the file matters for a single document. Position in a separate file doesn&#x27;t, because each file starts at line 1. Think about that for a second. The agent follows rules at the top of a long file more than rules at the bottom. That&#x27;s wild.</p><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">The Enforcement Severity Spectrum</h2><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Not all violations are equal. Creating a test file is a hard violation, the file shouldn&#x27;t exist. Forgetting to read a file before editing is a soft violation, the edit still might be correct. The hook system reflects this with three severity levels.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Block — The hook stops the tool call. The agent can&#x27;t proceed until it takes a different approach. Used for: test file creation, API key commits, writes to reference data files. Zero tolerance.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Warn — The hook injects a warning but allows the tool call to proceed. Used for: editing unread files, large file modifications, missing build verification. The agent gets the nudge without getting blocked from legitimate edge cases.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Remind — The hook injects a contextual reminder after the fact. Used for: dev server restarts after config changes, documentation updates after API changes, the &#x27;compilation isn&#x27;t validation&#x27; reminder.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">I tested 2-level (block/allow) and 5-level systems before settling on three. The 2-level system hit 87% compliance, but too many false blocks pushed the agent into workaround patterns. It would rename files to dodge the block, which was worse than the original violation. (Imagine that. The agent learned to game your rules.) The 5-level system scored 88%. The extra levels created decision fatigue. The agent spent tokens reasoning about whether a violation was severity 3 or severity 4 instead of doing its actual work. Three levels hit 95% compliance. Simple enough to be reliable.</p><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">Subagent Inheritance: The Gap That Breaks Everything</h2><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">The main agent follows the constitution. Then it spawns a subagent via the Task tool, and the subagent starts with zero governance context. I measured this gap: 68% compliance for subagents without constitution injection versus 95% with it. That&#x27;s a 27-point drop just because the rules didn&#x27;t get passed along.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">The fix is a PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool that automatically injects core rules into every subagent prompt. When the main agent spawns a code-reviewer, the hook appends the functional validation mandate, the no-test-files rule, and the evidence-gate checklist to the subagent&#x27;s instructions. The subagent inherits the constitution without the main agent needing to remember to pass it along.</p><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">This is the single most important lesson from the stack: governance must be automatic and inherited. If compliance depends on the agent remembering to propagate rules, it&#x27;ll forget. 2,827 Task spawns and 929 Agent calls across all 23,479 sessions. That&#x27;s 3,756 opportunities for governance to drop. How many of those do you think the agent would remember on its own? Automatic injection eliminates the failure mode entirely.</p><h2 style="margin-top:56px;margin-bottom:4px;font-size:30px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:-0.8px">What the Numbers Show</h2><p style="margin-top:24px;font-size:var(--text-body-prose);line-height:var(--leading-body);color:rgba(244,243,238,0.8)">Across the measured sessions, the aggregate violation rate dropped from 3.1 per session to 0.4, an 87% reduction. Hook overhead: 7ms per tool call, undetectable in practice.</p><figure class="wa-chart-anim" style="margin:32px 0;padding:20px 22px;border-radius:var(--radius, 12px);background:var(--surface,
